heading: 1 Introduction (1.1 Background, 1.2 Restatement of the Problem, 1.3 Our Work)
note: 12 blocks, 496 words, 12 printed units. 25 is the framing lead and it is pure scene-setting — Utah arches, Kilimanjaro, the Great Barrier Reef replaced by hurricanes, African famine and Tuvalu, with no number except none at all. 26 introduces green GDP and asks “whether GGDP is the most appropriate”, tail-carrying the “1.2 Restatement of the Problem” heading. 27 is the task lead and 28-31 are four of the five restated tasks, one block each (choose and analyse a GGDP method; predict the global climate impact; compare advantages and disadvantages; analyse one country), while 32 carries the fifth task and the “1.3 Our Work” heading in its tail. 33-36 are the four work paragraphs, one per task: 33 names the Mirković method, 34 the event-conditioned forecast plus three-level fuzzy evaluation, 35 the two-dimensional game, 36 Australia plus PVAR, and 36's tail carries “Figure 1: Our Work / 2 Model Preparation / 2.1 Assumptions and Justification”. Front matter is not coded: block 1 is the title line “GDP,Green planet”, 2-8 the 340-word Summary, and 9-24 the keywords and three pages of table-of-contents lines that the extractor split into one block per pointer row.

heading: 2.1 Assumptions and Justification
note: 3 blocks, 183 words, three assumption-plus-justification pairs, each printed as a single paragraph: countries will plan strictly by the new GGDP criteria (37); the world sees no further regional conflict, war or economic crisis in the horizon (38); and under current policy the energy structure and resource-use efficiency will not change significantly in the short run (39). The first is the load-bearing one, since the shift is modelled as a change in the evaluation criterion alone; the third is what licenses holding f and b constant in equation (16) later. Block 39's tail glues “2.2 Glossary / Table 1: Glossary” plus the first two rows (ECO2 in kt, Waste), so the glossary header is coded with this chapter and the table body with the next one.

heading: 2.2 Glossary (Table 1)
note: 5 blocks, 56 words. 40-43 are the remaining Table 1 rows, cut at row boundaries that do not align with block boundaries: 40 ends mid-row with “kt NRR”, 41 begins the NRR row, 42 carries the RGG row plus the three B indicators, and 43 finishes with “The Balance of the Ecosystem”. The glossary is nine symbols only (ECO2, Waste, NRR, RGG, B1, B2, B3) and none of the symbols the models actually use — Cp, Cw, Cr, Elect, Pelect, MPC, and every game and PVAR symbol — appears here. 44 is the table note, “There are some variables that are not listed in Table 1 and will be discussed in detail in each section”, which is a scope disclaimer rather than a definition.

heading: 3 Task 1: GGDP — An environmental prism through which to view economy / 3.1 Selection of pollution indicators
note: 11 blocks, 717 words. 45 is the section heading alone. 46 is the framing argument (traditional GDP ignores depleted resources and pollution), and 47 is the actual method choice: “this paper refers to a report published by Dr. Mijo Mirkovi´c in 2017[2], with some improvements based on it” — the select job, and the only place the method is attributed. 48 states what the method adds: the waste-to-energy principle plus a separation of actual damage cost from opportunity cost. 49-54 then build the three subtractions one at a time, each with its heading glued into the tail of the previous block: air treatment Cp = ECO2 × MPC with the CDM price of $11.07 per tonne in 2006 inflation-adjusted to other years (50-51); waste opportunity cost Cw with the 10-billion-tonne world waste figure and the conversion “one thousand tons of waste is converted into 74,000 kWh” (52-53); and the natural-resource term, total rents as a share of GDP times GDP (54). 55 is the data statement: World Bank and OECD, 46 countries over 1995-2020, one shorthand list of indicators, and “we take linear function to fill in” for missing ECO2 and Waste. Note the waste conversion is written “74,000 kWh per thousand tons”, which puts the electricity yield of a tonne of waste at 74 kWh — an order of magnitude above real waste-to-energy plants and the single number that drives the Cw term.

heading: 3.2 Calculation of GGDP
note: 3 blocks, 61 words. 56 is the one-line lead (“Then, based on the indicator GDP, the GGDP is calculated as follows”). 57 prints both equations in a single block — GGDP = GDP − ECO2×MPC/100 − Waste×Elect×Pelect − GDP×NRR as (1) and RGG = GGDP/GDP×100% as (2) — where the extraction mangles the SUVAT-style fraction. 58 defines the symbols and fixes the range: “the larger the RGG is, the greener the economy of a country, and the range of values is [0,1]”. Two printed inconsistencies belong here: equation (1) writes the second term as Waste×Elect×Pelect with no divisor while the text of 53 derived Elect as kWh per thousand tonnes of waste, so the term carries a hidden factor of 1000; and NRR is defined in the glossary as a percentage but used undivided in (1), which would subtract the whole of GDP whenever resource rents reach one percent. The stated [0,1] range is therefore not guaranteed by the printed formula.

heading: 3.3 GGDP calculation results
note: 2 blocks, 85 words. 59 announces the figure and its caption in one block (“The 46 country RGG is shown below. Figure 2: RGG of 46 countries.”). 60 is the whole result: developed countries in Western Europe and the United States have higher RGG, most developing countries lower, and resource-rich countries such as Russia and the Middle East lowest. Not one of the 46 values is printed in the text, so every number used later (Australia 93.74%, world 98.44% in 6 and 198) has to be recovered from the Figure 2 raster. The ordering claim is also stated as a rule with no counter-example discussion: if any single resource exporter had a high ratio the sentence would need qualification, and the paper does not say how many of the 46 fall outside the pattern.

heading: 4 Task2: Global climate mitigation of adopting GGDP / 4.1 Forecasting GGDP changes
note: 11 blocks, 469 words. 61-62 are the two headings. 63 is the modelling premise and it is an assumption, not a finding: “the impact of GGDP standard adoption on GDP is negligible, and its impact is mainly reflected in Cp, Cw and Cr”, justified only by the observation that GDP accounting still dominates. 64 fixes the counterfactual — the standard is assumed implemented at the start of 2021 in every country, and time-series plus linear fitting project the natural growth of each indicator to 2040 — and 65 is a stray heading fragment (“Cp,Cw,Cr changes after the adoption of GGDP. 4.1.1”). 66 is the only quantitative step: the policy effect is borrowed from the CO2 growth-rate change after the 2007-08 financial crisis and the Sichuan earthquake, and the policy impact factor “θ is 3%”, so growth rate = natural rate + θ, which 68 restates after Figure 3. 69 makes the GDP forecast a separate linear fit, 70 announces Figure 4, and 71 reads it: most countries improve, resource producers most, therefore GGDP “can significantly mitigate climate change”. The θ = 3% figure is asserted without a derivation, an interval or a sensitivity run in this chapter, and it is the single parameter that produces every forecast in section 4.

heading: 4.2 Fuzzy integrated evaluation model for climate improvement (4.2.1-4.2.3)
note: 39 blocks, 757 words, and the worst block fragmentation in the paper: blocks 75-86 are bare 10-17 word line fragments of three prose paragraphs, because the extractor cut each line at the 9pt column. The model itself is simple and worth recording exactly. Three indicators: global temperature B1, environmental pollution B2, ecosystem balance B3, each given a paragraph of motivation rather than a measurement (74-86). Four rubric levels: Green, Sub-Green, Normal, Bad (89-93), defined against the 2020 distribution of the 46 countries rather than against any absolute standard — Normal is literally “average of current climate protection in 2020”. Equations (3)-(6) build a data matrix D (3×46), a quantile matrix Q of minimum and three quartiles, a piecewise-linear membership function for each level, and the aggregate β = Weight·A. The AHP weight vectors are printed as (7): WB1 = (0.7402, 0.0757, 0.1840), WB2 = (0.0955, 0.6542, 0.2502), WB3 = (0.1428, 0.1428, 0.7142) — the third row is suspiciously exactly a repeat of 1/7, 1/7, 5/7, and no comparison matrix, eigenvalue or consistency ratio is printed anywhere for these three vectors, which makes them unverifiable in a way the 2023-2305794 AHP weights are not. 104-106 aggregate the 46 country vectors by GDP share into a world vector and define Score = 2w1 + 1w2 − 1w4 with range [−1, 2], silently dropping w3; the score scale therefore depends on w3 being small, which is never checked. 108-110 report that scores move toward (2, 2, 2) with GGDP.

heading: 5 Task 3: It's time to make the right choice / 5.1 Spatial dimension of the game (5.1.1 Game players, 5.1.2 Game rules, 5.1.3 Game start)
note: 45 measured blocks, 1047 words, 20 coded units over 21 printed items (the two player lists share one group); the chapter opens with two lead paragraphs before the game proper. 111 closes section 4 (“the climate crisis ... will be significantly mitigated when countries adopt GGDP”) and names the two obstacles the game has to answer — equity across countries and the short-versus-long-term benefit comparison — and 112 states the plan (a comparison in both spatial and temporal dimensions). 113 is the 5.1 heading, 114-115 set out the conflict (resource-dependent losers become opponents; the open question is whether mitigation compensates them or supporters buy them off) — nearly every bullet is a two-to-eight-block line-wrapped fragment. The player classification is by NRR and it is the cleanest construction in the paper: the five opponents are Iran, Saudi Arabia, Russia, Australia and Brazil, the seven supporters Iceland, Luxembourg, Switzerland, Belgium, France, Spain and Greece, the rest neutral (116-118). Note that Australia is listed as an opponent here, which is the same country the paper later recommends should adopt the standard, and that opposition is defined purely by resource dependence, so the losers are assumed to be the only objectors. The rules: a common disaster loss curve L, with Ln (no GGDP) and Ly (with GGDP) specified only as a normal-shaped expression in (10) whose parameters are never given; an international pressure term P = ln(αt) in (11) that decays with the number of games; and a subsidy pool S = Rs × p in (12) paid by supporters to the largest resource holder. Payoffs are F1 = −Ln and F2 = −Ln without GGDP, and F3 = −Ln − Rs×p, F4 = −Ln + P − ΔCr + Rs×p with it, condition (15) being F1 < F3 and F2 < F4, i.e. every country prefers the standard. Two things to flag: the supporters' payoff F3 is strictly worse than F1 by the subsidy they pay, so the condition F1 < F3 in (15) cannot hold as printed, and yet 151 asserts it for “any country”; and ΔCr in F4 is never defined. 154 is Table 2, the eight-year game result (R rejection, A acceptance, Y/N on continuing the subsidy), and 155 reads it as “after the 16th year ... all the opposing countries will agree”, a result that contradicts the summary's “within 15 years” and cannot be checked because the payoff parameters are unstated.

heading: 5.2 Trade-offs in the time dimension (5.2.1 Benefit calculation, 5.2.2 Factors of change, 5.2.3 Presentation of results)
note: 41 measured blocks, 763 words, 16 printed units. The device is a single scalar: Ec = t × v × f − b (16), the value extracted from the remaining environmental carrying capacity, with t time, v the transformation rate, f the transformation efficiency and b the policy effect. Vn = 12.0705t + 1299.8920 (17) is fitted to the historical world resource-use series and is the only estimated parameter in the chapter. 163 then states the physical closure of the model — resources have an upper limit, so once v pushes t to the limit benefits stop rising, and f and b are held constant — which is what makes the exercise finite. 165-192 lists the five channels through which GGDP changes the parameters, one bullet each, and here the equations are decorations rather than derivations: Δf = 1/(1+e^-t) (18) for clean-energy diffusion, Δf = Σ(sin i + 1) (19) for firm-level efficiency gains, fs = σ/t (20) for welfare subsidies, vi = −Σ λ^i/i! (21) for the corrected externality, and m, the treatment cost, for which no equation is given at all. None of these has a fitted coefficient; σ, λ and the summation ranges are unstated, and (21) is printed with a minus sign on a sum of positive terms, so vi would always be negative, i.e. resource use decreasing even before any policy. 193-196 gives Ec1 and Ec2 in (22)-(23), with 194-195 splitting Ec2 across two blocks mid-formula, and 196 is the Figure 9 caption (“Total global natural resource income before and after the adoption of GGDP”). The comparison is therefore between two curves of unknown magnitude; the paper never prints the crossing year or the size of the gap.

heading: 6 Task 4: Australia's economic health diagnosis under GGDP criteria (lead)
note: 3 blocks, 142 words. 197 is the section heading; 198 is the diagnostic finding and the only place Australia's own numbers appear: “Australia's RGG in 2020 is 93.74%, while the world average score in the same period is at 98.44%”, which the paper reads as high pollution, below-average performance, low waste utilisation and over-reliance on resource extraction. 199 compares Australia with Germany — “Australia has a high level of waste and low utilization of waste” — and concludes that GGDP adoption would help. Neither 93.74% nor 98.44% appears in the text of section 3, so both are quoted here without an intermediate working step; and the 4.7-point gap is small enough that the “does not reach the world average” verdict rests on a difference the paper never tests against measurement error in the four input indicators.

heading: 6.1 Industrial transformation to reduce overexploitation of resources (6.1.1 PVAR, 6.1.2 Analysis of results)
note: 27 blocks, 1207 words, 22 printed units — the only chapter in the paper with a full, textbook-shaped estimation chain, and it is seven explicit steps. 201-203 sets up the transformation with geography and mine closure (201 is description with no number, hence background). 205-207 gives the PVAR equation (24) and its symbol list; 208 names the three endogenous variables (ATI, MTI, TTI — total, secondary and tertiary factor income for eight regions, 1990-2020, all logged). 210-212 prints Table 3, the three unit-root tests, all rejecting at 1% in first differences. 214-215 prints Table 4 (lag order: MBIC, MAIC and MQIC all minimised at lag one) and 217 prints the unit-circle check with “all nine estimated points ... within the unit circle” — but the caption it refers to is “Figure 1”, which is the framework diagram at the start of the paper; the actual stability plot is Figure 10 (218). 221 reads Table 5: “MTI with one period lag has a significantly stronger positive shock to ATI ... and TTI with one period lag” has the same, and 222-224 reads Table 6, the variance decomposition — tertiary contribution 47.27% at the end against 31.66% own and the remainder for MTI. That 47.27% is the number the summary quotes. 225-226 draws the policy conclusion: suppressing part of the secondary sector “will not cause significant negative impact”, so mining should be closed in favour of tertiary industries. The step from a variance decomposition to a counterfactual closure of an industry is the largest inferential jump in the paper: a 47% variance share says tertiary shocks explain movements in growth, not that removing mining leaves growth intact, and the PVAR is estimated on 31 years of eight regions with no structural identification.

heading: 6.2 Waste Reuse
note: 7 blocks, 310 words. 227 is the comparison statement with numbers (Australia fourteenth largest waste producer, recycling “less than half”, Germany 83% in 2013 with 65% recycled and 18% incinerated), 228 is the Figure 11 caption, and 229-232 are the four arguments read off the figure, each with its own bold sub-label glued into the block: land occupation (an incineration plant 0.9 million square metres against a landfill's 67,000 — note the printed comparison points the wrong way for the argument being made, since the incineration plant occupies more land), greenhouse gases (Australia emits 5.88 million tonnes of methane and 3.528 million tonnes of CO2 from landfill a year), and the economic benefit of waste-to-energy (Germany gets 12% of its power from it). 233 draws the conclusion — follow Germany, raise recycling — and tail-carries “6.3 Policy Recommendations / CO2 emissions policy:”. The 0.9 million square metre figure for one plant against 67,000 for “a medium-sized landfill” is the one place where the paper's own numbers undercut its stated case, and no correction or reconciliation appears.

heading: 6.3 Policy Recommendations
note: 27 blocks, 306 words, eight printed units under three sub-headings. CO2 emissions policy: a carbon tax adjusted on public and enterprise feedback (234-235); a carbon-leakage guard for states with different tax rates (236-237); and a nature-based sequestration programme on the agriculture, forestry and livestock base with annual targets (238-240, whose tail carries “Waste disposal policy:”). Waste policy: a three-step landfill strategy — stop expanding, stop building, ban — with deadlines and monitoring (241-244), and cooperation with European countries on incineration and flue-gas treatment (245-248). Natural-resource policy: reduce mining damage and put the displaced workers on social subsidies while redeveloping abandoned mines as tourism (250-256), and promote innovation, renewables and nuclear while cutting direct coal combustion (257-260). Every item is a directive with no quantified target, no cost and no sequencing beyond the landfill steps, and the mining item is the concrete form of the PVAR conclusion from 6.1. 249 is the third sub-heading alone, hence `route` rather than `handoff`.

heading: 7 Model Evaluation and Further Discussion / 7.1 Sensitivity analysis
note: 3 blocks, 131 words. 261-262 are the two headings. 263 is the entire experiment: the policy impact factor θ is varied and the paper reports that “the relative relationship reflected by the results remains the same”, which is the only stability statement given. No value of θ other than the baseline 3% is printed, no table or figure accompanies the claim, and the parameters with the largest effect on the results — the AHP weight vectors of (7), the equal treatment of the three fuzzy indicators, the fitted Vn slope of 12.07 and the unstated σ, λ and p of section 5.2 — are not perturbed at all. Block 263's tail glues “7.2 Model Strengths”.

heading: 7.2 Model Strengths / 7.3 Model Weaknesses
note: 11 measured blocks, 132 words, four printed bullets. The two strengths are self-descriptions: indicators chosen scientifically, with data completeness compared across sites and “more complete raw data for 46 countries” compiled (264-267); and the model “makes full reference to the impact of real historical events and international rules” (268-270), which is the θ-borrowing from the 2007-08 crisis. The two weaknesses are real and specific: the model ignores water, land and biodiversity (271-272), and “There is a certain subjective element in the trend of our curve in the forecast of future policy impact” (273-274) — the same subjective element that produced the 3% policy factor and the unreported sensitivity of 263. 274's tail carries “A document to the Australian Government”, so the memo follows immediately with no separate conclusion chapter.

heading: A document to the Australian Government
note: 6 blocks, 467 words, a two-page letter after the weaknesses and before the references. 275 is the salutation (“To whom it may concern,”) and 276 is the self-introduction as “a policy steering team hired by ICM”, with the three new dimensions named (carbon dioxide emissions, unrecycled waste, resource dependence). 277 restates the PVAR result in plain language — tertiary highest contribution, mining still large but reserves finite — and 278 supplies the emotional case: “1,120 hectares of forest vegetation were burned by the 2019 Australian hill fires, killing 1.2 billion creatures”, with Pacific island nations at risk by 2050. 279 is the Germany comparison on landfill, recycling and conversion rates. 280 is the recommendation: set GGDP as the new standard, signed “Yours Sincerely”, with “References” in its tail. Two details to record: the memo says the analysis used “regression models”, where the body used a panel VAR; and the 1,120 hectares figure is far below the published burnt area of the 2019-20 season (about 17 million hectares), so the letter's most vivid number is off by four orders of magnitude.
